how-to-calculate-ifta-quarterly-tax.html.text:
How is IFTA quarterly tax calculated?

Four steps, one of which almost every hand-built worksheet gets wrong. Here is a full quarter for a two-truck carrier based in Illinois, worked line by line, ending in a return that owes money on a quarter whose fuel tax nets to a credit.

Open the calculator with this quarter loaded

The quarter

Two trucks, one Midwest lane, five jurisdictions. The rates below are illustrative — real ones come from the official IFTA rate table for the quarter being filed, which is why the calculator asks you for them rather than shipping a table that would be stale within weeks.

JurisdictionMilesGallons boughtTax rateSurcharge
IL8,4001,420.00$0.6270—
IN6,150380.00$0.3400$0.6200
KY4,820910.00$0.2160$0.1020
OH7,3101,180.00$0.4700—
MI2,6400.00$0.3130—
Total29,3203,890.00

Step 1 — one fleet MPG, for the whole fleet and the whole quarter

Every gallon figure on the return descends from this one number: total miles everywhere, over total gallons bought everywhere.

29,320 ÷ 3,890.00 = 7.54 MPG.

Two things about it are load-bearing. It is fleet-wide — there is no per-jurisdiction MPG, and computing one is the most common way a spreadsheet produces figures that look reasonable and reconcile to nothing. And it is carried to two decimals, because that is the figure the return itself carries; a worksheet that keeps full precision disagrees with the filed return by a few dollars per jurisdiction, which is small and is exactly the sort of unexplainable variance that lengthens an audit.

Step 2 — taxable gallons, from miles rather than from purchases

What a jurisdiction taxes is the fuel you burned inside it, which it works out from your miles and your fleet MPG. What you bought there is a separate figure entirely, and it arrives as a credit in step 3.

Michigan is the clearest case: 2,640 miles, not a drop of fuel bought. 2,640 ÷ 7.54 = 350.13 taxable gallons, every one of them owed at $0.3130 — $109.59.

Step 3 — net taxable gallons, and the tax that follows

Net taxable gallons are what you burned there less what you already paid tax on there. Negative means you bought more fuel in that state than you burned in it, and the state owes you.

Illinois: 1,114.06 burned − 1,420.00 bought = −305.94, at $0.6270 → a credit of $191.82. Ohio and Kentucky come back in credit too. Add the five tax lines together and the fuel tax on this quarter is a credit of $91.53.

At this point a carrier working from a spreadsheet concludes the quarter is a refund and files accordingly. It is not.

Step 4 — the surcharge, which is not another tax rate

Indiana, Kentucky and Virginia collect part of their diesel tax as a surcharge on the return rather than at the pump. Two properties make it behave unlike everything above:

  • It is charged on taxable gallons — the fuel you burned there — not on net taxable gallons.
  • There is nothing to credit against it. Fuel you bought in the state reduced the tax line; it does not touch this one.

Indiana: 815.65 taxable gallons × $0.6200 = $505.70. Kentucky: 639.26 × $0.1020 = $65.20. Together, $570.90.

Kentucky is the instructive one. Its tax line is a credit — 270.74 gallons in hand — and it still owes the surcharge in full. Model the surcharge as one more rate to be netted against that credit and you would compute −270.74 × $0.1020, a further credit, instead of a charge.

The return

JurisdictionTaxable galTax-paid galNet taxableTaxSurchargeRow total
IL1,114.061,420.00−305.94−$191.82—−$191.82
IN815.65380.00435.65$148.12$505.70$653.82
KY639.26910.00−270.74−$58.48$65.20$6.72
OH969.501,180.00−210.50−$98.94—−$98.94
MI350.130.00350.13$109.59—$109.59
Total−$91.53$570.90$479.37

The fuel tax is a credit of $91.53. The return owes $479.37. A worksheet that netted the surcharge would have reported $242.48 of surcharge instead of $570.90 — $328.42 short, in one quarter, on a return its author believed was a refund.

If the return is late

Interest accrues to each jurisdiction you owe, at one twelfth of the annual rate for every month or part of a month. A credit due back from another jurisdiction does not offset it. So a return that nets to a refund overall can still carry interest — on the quarter above, Indiana, Kentucky and Michigan would each accrue on their own row total, and Illinois and Ohio would accrue nothing and reduce nothing.

The three checks worth running before you file

Does the fleet MPG look like a truck?

A qualified vehicle usually returns somewhere between 3 and 12 MPG. Outside that band, the likeliest explanation is not a remarkable fleet: it is a jurisdiction's miles or gallons left out, miles and gallons entered in the wrong columns, or litres entered as gallons. Every taxable-gallon figure descends from this number, so an error here is an error in all of them.

Did you buy fuel where you ran no miles?

A purchase in a jurisdiction with no recorded miles is a standard audit query. Either the trip records are missing those miles, or the receipt belongs to a different state.

Is any rate still zero?

A jurisdiction with taxable miles and a rate of zero contributes nothing to the total and looks, on the page, exactly like a jurisdiction that has been dealt with.

Work your own quarter — free, in your browser

Other tools for the same desk: the owner-operator cost-per-mile calculator prices what a mile costs before you quote it, and the freight accessorial auditor checks whether an accessorial on an invoice was billed correctly.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it is not a filing. It makes no determination about what your base jurisdiction requires, which miles any jurisdiction exempts, whether your vehicle is qualified, what rate applies to your fuel type, or what you owe — and the rates used above are an illustrative example rather than a rate table. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own trip and fuel records, the official IFTA rate table for the quarter you are filing, and a qualified tax professional before you file from it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Your mileage, fuel purchases, jurisdictions and the figures worked out here are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and switched off automatically for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

Free and open source. MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

FOR SMALL CARRIERS AND OWNER-OPERATORS FILING THEIR OWN IFTA

The surcharge is not another tax rate.

Indiana, Kentucky and Virginia collect part of their diesel tax on the return instead of at the pump, and that part is charged on every taxable gallon you burned there — with no credit for fuel you bought there. On the quarter loaded below, the tax line across five jurisdictions nets to a credit of $91.53. The return owes $479.37. Model the surcharge as one more rate to be netted and you file $328.42 short, on a quarter you thought was a refund.

Put your own quarter in. Everything runs in this browser; nothing is uploaded and nothing is filed.

How is IFTA quarterly tax actually calculated? — the worked example, line by line

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet — the two rules a hand-built worksheet almost always gets wrong. Already using a paid prep service? See how this compares to ExpressIFTA.

Your quarter, jurisdiction by jurisdiction

One row per jurisdiction you ran in. Rates come from the official IFTA rate table for the quarter you are filing — this tool ships none, because they change quarterly in 58 jurisdictions and a stale rate in a filed return is the worst place to be wrong. Leave taxable miles blank unless the jurisdiction exempts some of them; blank means all miles are taxable. Leave surcharge blank unless the jurisdiction levies one.

Jurisdiction Total miles Taxable miles Tax-paid gallons Tax rate $/gal Surcharge $/gal

This quarter is saved automatically to this browser, so it is still here on your next visit — “Clear the example” erases both the fields and the saved copy. “Copy a link” puts every row and both late-filing fields into the URL after the #, which is never sent to a server or logged anywhere, so sending it to a bookkeeper or co-owner uploads nothing.

If the return is late

Leave both at zero for an on-time return. Interest accrues to each jurisdiction you owe, at one twelfth of the annual rate per month or part month — a credit somewhere else does not offset it, which is why a return that nets to a refund can still carry interest. The annual rate is set for the calendar year by the International Fuel Tax Association; take it from there rather than from here.

The return, line by line

This is the shape of the jurisdiction schedule on an IFTA return. Taxable gallons come from your fleet MPG, not from what you bought in the state; the surcharge column is charged on taxable gallons with nothing credited against it.

      Common questions

      How do you calculate IFTA taxable gallons?

      Taxable gallons in a jurisdiction are that jurisdiction’s taxable miles divided by the average MPG of your whole fleet across the whole quarter — not the gallons you bought there. On the worked example this page opens with, the fleet ran 29,320 miles on 3,890 gallons, so its average is 7.54 MPG, and Indiana’s 6,150 miles become 815.65 taxable gallons whether the truck fuelled there or not. Computing a separate MPG per jurisdiction is the most common way a hand-built worksheet produces figures that look reasonable and reconcile to nothing.

      Why does my IFTA return say I owe money when I have a fuel credit?

      Almost always the surcharge. Indiana, Kentucky and Virginia collect part of their diesel tax as a surcharge on the return rather than at the pump, and it is charged on all your taxable gallons in that state with no credit for fuel you bought there. On the worked example the tax line across five jurisdictions nets to a credit of $91.53 — and the return still owes $479.37, because the surcharge adds $570.90 that no amount of fuel buying reduces. A worksheet that treats the surcharge as another tax rate, netted against the credit, reports $242.48 instead: a $328.42 understatement in a single quarter.

      Does buying more fuel in Kentucky reduce my surcharge?

      No, and this is the part that costs carriers money in both directions. Buying fuel in a surcharge state reduces the tax line, because tax-paid gallons are credited against taxable gallons. It does nothing whatever to the surcharge line, which is charged on taxable gallons — the fuel you burned there — regardless of where you bought it. So fuel-buying strategy moves one of the two lines and not the other, and any plan built on the assumption that it moves both will be wrong by the whole surcharge.

      What tax rates should I use?

      The ones on the official IFTA rate table for the specific quarter you are filing, which is published by the International Fuel Tax Association and republished by every base jurisdiction. This calculator deliberately ships no rate table. Rates change every quarter across 58 jurisdictions and some change mid-quarter, so a table baked into a tool would be stale within weeks and stale in the worst possible place — a filed tax return. Enter the rate and, where one applies, the surcharge rate for your fuel type, and the arithmetic is yours to check.

      What counts as taxable miles versus total miles?

      Total miles is every mile the qualified vehicle ran in that jurisdiction. Taxable miles is that figure less any miles the jurisdiction exempts — the exemptions vary by jurisdiction and typically cover things like some toll miles, fuel-trip-permit miles, and certain off-highway use. Most carriers have no exempt miles at all, so leaving the taxable column blank here means all the miles are taxable. Exempt miles come off the taxable line but stay in the fleet MPG, because the fleet really did drive them on the fuel it really did burn. What each jurisdiction exempts is its determination, not this tool’s.

      Do I still owe interest if my return nets to a refund?

      Yes, if you filed late. IFTA interest accrues to each jurisdiction you owe tax to, at one twelfth of the annual rate for each month or part of a month, and a credit due back from another jurisdiction does not offset it. That is why this calculator computes interest on the jurisdictions in debit alone rather than on the netted total, and flags the case where a return in overall credit still carries interest. The annual rate is set for the calendar year and published by the International Fuel Tax Association — enter it rather than reading one from this page, for the same reason the tax rates are inputs.

      Do I need to file IFTA if I only ran in one state?

      IFTA covers qualified vehicles operating in two or more member jurisdictions, so a quarter run entirely inside your base jurisdiction may not need a return — but most base jurisdictions require licensees to file every quarter regardless, including a zero return. This calculator flags a return with a single jurisdiction rather than assuming either way, because what your licence obliges you to file is a question for your base jurisdiction and not one arithmetic can answer.

      Is any of this uploaded?

      No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your mileage, your fuel purchases, the jurisdictions you run and the figures worked out from them are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

      Can I save this quarter or send it to someone else?

      Yes. Your rows and both late-filing fields are saved to this browser automatically, so they are still here on your next visit. The copy-link button puts the same figures into the page’s own address after the #, which is never sent to a server or logged anywhere, so opening that link reopens the exact return and sending it uploads nothing.

      Is this tax advice, and can I file from it?

      No to both. It is a worksheet: arithmetic on figures you type, using rates you supply. It is not tax advice and it is not a filing — it files nothing, transmits nothing, and makes no determination about what your base jurisdiction requires, which miles a jurisdiction exempts, whether your vehicle is qualified, or what you owe. Your base jurisdiction assesses the return. Check every figure against your own trip and fuel records and the official rate table, and ask a qualified tax professional before you file from it.

      No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it is not a filing. It makes no determination about what your base jurisdiction requires, which miles any jurisdiction exempts, whether your vehicle is qualified, what rate applies to your fuel type, or what you owe — and the rates it opens with are an illustrative example rather than a rate table. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own trip and fuel records, the official IFTA rate table for the quarter you are filing, and a qualified tax professional before you file from it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

      Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Your mileage, fuel purchases, jurisdictions and the figures worked out here are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and switched off automatically for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control. This quarter is saved to this browser’s own storage so it is here next visit, and “Copy a link to this quarter” carries the same figures in the page’s own address after the # — never a query string a server would log, never uploaded, and readable only by whoever you send it to.

      Tracking days away from home for your meal deduction? The owner-operator per diem calculator compares per diem with receipts and estimates the tax saved.

      Working out what a mile actually costs you before you quote it? The owner-operator cost-per-mile calculator prices the truck. Checking whether an accessorial on a freight invoice was billed correctly? Try the freight accessorial auditor. Driving for an app rather than under your own authority? The gig driver net pay calculator is the one for that.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← IFTA Quarterly Fuel Tax Calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

An IFTA return is arithmetic, and a spreadsheet can do arithmetic. What a hand-built worksheet usually gets wrong is not the arithmetic but two specific rules the return applies: fleet-wide MPG, and a surcharge that no fuel credit ever reduces.

Where a hand-built worksheet usually goes wrong

RuleCommon spreadsheet shortcutWhat this calculator does
Fleet MPGDivides each jurisdiction's own miles by its own gallons, producing a different MPG per row.Divides total fleet miles by total fleet gallons once, and applies that single MPG to every jurisdiction's taxable miles.
The surchargeApplies the surcharge rate to each jurisdiction's net taxable gallons, so a fuel credit there quietly reduces it.Applies the surcharge rate to gross taxable gallons burned in that jurisdiction, with no credit for fuel bought there, exactly as the return requires.
Plausibility checksNone, unless someone remembers to add one -- a wrong MPG or a zero-rate jurisdiction looks like any other number in a cell.Flags an average MPG outside the 3–12 realistic band, fuel bought with no recorded miles, taxable miles at a zero rate, and a return in net credit that still owes interest.
Does anything I type get uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The return runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is sent to a server.

What the two mistakes cost, on the calculator's own worked example

The quarter this calculator opens with runs 29,320 miles on 3,890 gallons across five jurisdictions, for a fleet-wide average of 7.54 MPG. Indiana's 6,150 miles become 815.65 taxable gallons at that rate, owing $653.82 in tax and surcharge together. A worksheet that instead divides Indiana's own 6,150 miles by the 380 gallons bought there gets 16.18 MPG — outside the 3–12 MPG band a qualified vehicle realistically returns — and reports Indiana's taxable gallons as just 380.1, for a total of $235.69. That single jurisdiction alone is understated by $418.13.

Across all five jurisdictions, the tax line nets to a credit of $91.53, and the Indiana/Kentucky surcharge adds $570.90 that no fuel credit reduces, so the return owes $479.37. A worksheet that instead applies each surcharge rate to that jurisdiction's own net taxable gallons — letting a credit in Kentucky quietly reduce the surcharge owed there — totals $150.95: a $328.42 understatement from one modeling choice, on a return that nets to a fraction of what is actually owed.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Open the IFTA Quarterly Fuel Tax Calculator to work your own quarter, or see how this compares to a paid preparation service like ExpressIFTA.

Common questions

Isn't an IFTA return just arithmetic I can do in a spreadsheet?

Yes -- it is arithmetic, and a spreadsheet can do arithmetic. What trips up a hand-built worksheet is not the arithmetic itself but two specific rules the return applies that a spreadsheet has to be told to apply: fleet MPG is one number computed fleet-wide, not per jurisdiction, and a surcharge is charged on every taxable gallon burned in that jurisdiction with no credit for fuel bought there, however the tax line nets out. Skip either rule and the numbers still look reasonable -- they just do not reconcile to what an audit finds.

How much does computing MPG per jurisdiction actually cost me?

On the worked example this calculator opens with, the fleet ran 29,320 miles on 3,890 gallons for a fleet-wide average of 7.54 MPG, and Indiana's 6,150 miles become 815.65 taxable gallons at that rate, owing $653.82 in tax and surcharge combined. A worksheet that instead divides Indiana's own 6,150 miles by the 380 gallons bought there gets 16.18 MPG -- outside the 3-12 MPG band a qualified vehicle realistically returns -- and reports Indiana's taxable gallons as just 380.1, a debit of three cents in tax plus the surcharge on that smaller gallon figure, $235.69 in total. That single jurisdiction alone is understated by $418.13 in one quarter.

How much does netting the surcharge against a credit cost me?

On the same worked example, the tax line across all five jurisdictions nets to a credit of $91.53, and the surcharge (Indiana and Kentucky both charge one) adds $570.90 that no fuel credit reduces, for a return that owes $479.37. A worksheet that instead applies each surcharge rate to that jurisdiction's own net taxable gallons -- so a credit in Kentucky quietly reduces the surcharge owed there -- totals $150.95: a $328.42 understatement from one modeling choice.

So why not just build the fleet-wide MPG and surcharge rules into my own spreadsheet?

You can, and a correctly built one gets the same answer this calculator does -- it is the same arithmetic either way. What a spreadsheet will not do on its own is flag the mistakes that produce a plausible-looking wrong answer: an average MPG outside the realistic band, fuel bought in a jurisdiction with no recorded miles, taxable miles sitting at a zero rate, or a credit-in-total return that still owes interest. This calculator runs those checks on every submission; a spreadsheet only runs the checks someone remembered to add.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it is not a filing. It makes no determination about what your base jurisdiction requires, which miles any jurisdiction exempts, whether your vehicle is qualified, what rate applies to your fuel type, or what you owe — and the figures on this page are an illustrative example rather than a rate table. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every figure against your own trip and fuel records, the official IFTA rate table for the quarter you are filing, and a qualified tax professional before you file from it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Your mileage, fuel purchases, jurisdictions and the figures worked out here are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count.

Free and open source. If it saves you a quarter’s worth of arguing with a spreadsheet, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-expressifta.html.text:
← IFTA Quarterly Fuel Tax Calculator

This calculator vs. ExpressIFTA

Two different shapes: ExpressIFTA is a paid, account-based service that holds a fuel-tax rate table for you and generates the state-specific return. This is a free, private, no-account browser worksheet that ships no rate table on purpose and exists to catch the surcharge-netting error and the transcription mistakes an IFTA audit looks for.

What each tool is for

ExpressIFTA, from ExpressTruckTax / SPAN Enterprises, is an IFTA return preparation service. Entering your mileage and fuel data costs nothing; generating the actual jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction return costs $24.95 per quarterly filing, regardless of how many vehicles are on it, with no separate monthly subscription. It requires creating an account and entering your business and vehicle details. It carries a fuel tax rate table that it updates itself each quarter, along with trip-sheet entry and GPS-upload features for building up your mileage record. It prepares a state-specific return for you to review and file — it does not submit that return to your base jurisdiction on your behalf; you remain the filer.

This calculator does none of what ExpressIFTA does. It does not hold your trip history, take a GPS feed, keep an account, or maintain a rate table. Given the miles and gallons you have already pulled together per jurisdiction — from trip sheets, an ELD export, or fuel-card statements — and this quarter's rates from the official IFTA sheet, it computes fleet-wide average MPG, taxable and net taxable gallons per jurisdiction, the Indiana/Kentucky/Virginia surcharge charged on every taxable gallon burned there with no credit for fuel bought there, interest on a late return accrued per jurisdiction owed, and three checks aimed at the errors an IFTA audit looks for: an implausible fleet MPG, fuel bought where no miles were recorded, and taxable miles sitting at a zero rate. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want a service that keeps a current rate table and generates my state-specific IFTA return.ExpressIFTA, or a comparable paid IFTA filing service — that is what it is built for.
I already have my per-jurisdiction miles and gallons and want an instant check on the surcharge and the common transcription errors, without an account.This calculator — free, private, no sign-up.
Does my return understate what I owe by netting a surcharge state against a fuel-tax credit somewhere else?This calculator's surcharge-gap panel, which quotes the exact shortfall.
What is my fleet's average MPG this quarter, computed the way the return requires?This calculator, fleet-wide across every jurisdiction entered.
I need trip-sheet entry, a GPS mileage feed, or an account my whole office can use across quarters.ExpressIFTA or a comparable service — this calculator keeps no history and no account.
How does the math behind an IFTA quarterly return actually work?This calculator's own worked example.
Do I need to create an account or pay to use the tool?This calculator: no, for either. ExpressIFTA: an account, and $24.95 to generate the return.

Most carriers who file their own IFTA get different value from each: ExpressIFTA (or a comparable paid service) for a maintained rate table and a generated, filing-ready return across quarters, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login gut-check on the surcharge and the transcription errors before you commit to a return — whichever tool produces the numbers you actually file.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ExpressIFTA?

They solve different parts of the same quarter. ExpressIFTA, from ExpressTruckTax/SPAN Enterprises, is a paid, account-based service: you enter your trip and fuel data for free, and it charges $24.95 per quarterly return (regardless of fleet size, no subscription) to generate your state-specific IFTA return, using a fuel-tax rate table it updates itself each quarter. It does not file the return with your base jurisdiction for you — you still submit what it prepares. This calculator does one narrower thing for free, with no account: given the miles and gallons you already pulled from your trip sheets or fuel-card statements, it works out fleet MPG, taxable and net taxable gallons per jurisdiction, the Indiana/Kentucky/Virginia surcharge charged the way it is actually charged — on every taxable gallon burned there, with no credit for fuel bought there — and flags three data-entry errors an IFTA audit looks for. It ships no rate table on purpose: you type in this quarter's rate from the official sheet, so nothing here can go stale between quarters. A carrier who wants a service to hold their rate table and produce the filing paperwork is better served by ExpressIFTA or a comparable provider. A carrier who has their miles and gallons in hand and wants an instant, private check on the surcharge and the common transcription errors before they file is in the right place here.

Does ExpressIFTA handle the surcharge correctly?

This page does not know, and does not claim to. ExpressIFTA's own marketing describes automatic per-jurisdiction rate updates and accurate fuel tax calculations; it does not publish enough detail in public view to confirm how it nets a surcharge state against a fuel-tax credit elsewhere. What is verifiable is the error this calculator exists to catch: a return that treats a state's surcharge as an ordinary tax rate, netted against that state's fuel credit, understates what is owed — $328.42 on the worked example this calculator opens with, because a surcharge applies to every taxable gallon burned there with nothing credited back. Whichever tool you use, check that its surcharge line survives being netted against a credit before you file from it.

Do I need an account to use either one?

For ExpressIFTA, yes: its own site describes creating an account and entering your business and vehicle details before you can generate a return. This calculator needs no account and no sign-in — it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and it keeps working with the connection off once it has loaded.

Why doesn't this calculator ship a rate table the way ExpressIFTA does?

Because a rate table baked into a free, rarely-updated static page goes stale, and IFTA rates change every quarter across 58 jurisdictions, sometimes mid-quarter. ExpressIFTA is a maintained paid service and can credibly promise to keep its table current; a tool like this one cannot make that promise honestly, so instead of guessing it asks you to type in the rate and surcharge from the official quarterly sheet for the jurisdictions you actually ran in. That is more typing than a service with a built-in table asks for, and it is the trade this calculator makes on purpose rather than the trade every filer wants.

Is this page affiliated with ExpressIFTA?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ExpressIFTA, ExpressTruckTax, or SPAN Enterprises. ExpressIFTA is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
